1:
The venture is read as faith, and as irregularity. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) makes Jonathan the typical warrior of a wild and adventurous age, recklessly brave and generous, animated by an intense faith in the willingness and power of the Eternal to help Israel — the mainspring, he says, of every great Hebrew hero from Joshua to David, and the thing King Saul utterly lacked, hence his rejection; he quotes Bishop Hall on the divine power of faith that makes a man more than men, since the question is not what Jonathan can do but what God can do, whose power lies not in the means but in Himself. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says plainly that the action was totally contrary to the laws of war, no military operation being undertaken without the general’s knowledge, and allows it only as led by a divine influence. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) grants the maxim about saving by many or by few readily in general and finds it hard to apply in particular: to believe that God can not only save us but save by us, when we are few and feeble, is the instance of faith. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) ground the resolution in the conviction that Israel was the nation of God.

Where the father waited is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch take Rimmon for an appellative noun, a pomegranate-tree, and deny it is the rock Rimmon; Clarke and Henry take it the other way, as the strong rock in which six hundred Benjamites once sheltered, Henry supposing Saul hidden in that very rock, so mean and abject was his spirit now. Ellicott instead notes the Israelite love of trees and lets the pomegranate stand. Henry makes the sending for priest and ark a deserted prince courting a deserted priest, and remarks that those who have lost the substance of religion are fondest of its shadows. On the priest himself Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) identify Ahiah with the Ahimelech later murdered at Nob, the one name meaning friend of the Eternal and the other brother of the king; Keil and Delitzsch allow instead that Ahimelech may have been his brother, succeeding him because he died without sons. John Gill (reformed) corrects the genealogy: Ahitub, not Ahiah, was Ichabod’s brother, and Ahiah was Ahitub’s son.

The two crags and the sign are handled closely. Clarke gives the Targum’s glosses, slippery and treading down; Ellicott calls the names of extreme antiquity and their meaning disputed, possibly shining and the acacia, and notes the rocks have been identified by modern travellers; Gill reports the Targum deriving Bozez from its being lubricous. Wesley guards against a misreading: the rocks were not one on each hand of the pass, or Jonathan could have walked between them, but one toothed northward toward Michmash and the other southward toward Gibeah, so that he had to climb over both. Keil and Delitzsch judge the sign well chosen — wait till we come would have shown courage, come up to us cowardice — and defend it as no tempting of God, since he acted in the exercise of his calling and not for himself. Wesley notes that such extraordinary impulses were divers among great and good men in ancient times.

On the trembling that followed they divide. Gill has the two follow their blows so quickly that twenty fell in a very little time and a very small space of ground; Ellicott holds the earthquake literal and far the best reading, the powers of nature summoned as at the Red Sea and Beth-horon; Keil and Delitzsch have the ground quake with the noise and tumult of the frightened foe, the whole growing into a trembling of God; Clarke thinks it probably a metaphor for commotion, allowing that God might have produced a real one.
16:
What the watchmen saw is textually obscure. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) survey the readings of the clause rendered they went on beating down one another: the Rabbins are unanimous for more and more was it broken up, taking the second word as an infinitive absolute; Gesenius gives it the sense of being dissolved and scattered; others read it adverbially, supplying a correlate to yield hither and thither, as the Septuagint does, which leaves the first verb untranslated. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) judges the Rabbinical reading the best of these and renders it were more and more broken up; he adds that the camps lay only two miles apart with a deep ravine between, so the panic spreading from outpost to main body was plainly visible. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reports the Vulgate’s quite different sense, that the multitude were prostrate.

Then comes the chapter’s sharpest textual question: whether the king called for the ark or the ephod. Ellicott sets out the case for the ephod at length. The Septuagint reads bring hither the ephod, for he bore the ephod in those days; no hint elsewhere suggests the sacred coffer ever left Kiriath-jearim before David bore it to Zion; the verb here used is never used of the ark; and no oracle could be asked of or by the ark, the Urim and Thummim by which answers were given belonging to the high-priestly ephod. He concludes that the Greek probably represents the original, that the Hebrew with ark is nevertheless of extreme antiquity, and that the explanatory second clause is most likely an ancient scribe’s gloss; Josephus, who has the priest take the garment of his high priesthood and prophesy, plainly had the shorter text. He reports and rejects Maurer’s defence of the Hebrew — that the king wanted not an oracle but the encouragement of the ark’s presence — as sinking him to the level of the sons of Eli, who carried the ark out and lost it. Keil and Delitzsch are struck by the same expression and press the same improbability, that the ark was then at Kirjath-jearim and would hardly be in so small a camp, and that elsewhere the high priest inquiring of God is associated with the ephod and not with the ark. John Gill (reformed) simply notes the Greek reading and that Kimchi understood the ephod with its Urim and Thummim.

On the order to withdraw the hand Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) offers two readings and guards against a third: either the king thought the case now plain enough, or he would not wait for an answer, being in such haste to fight a falling enemy; but he would have been very unwise indeed if he forbade the lifting up of hands in prayer, since Moses continued to lift up his while Joshua was engaged with Amalek. Keil and Delitzsch render it flatly, draw thy hand in, leave off now. Henry also turns the enemy’s advantage against them: they had been secure because all the swords and spears were theirs, and God made their own weapons the instruments of their destruction.

The turncoats raise one more variant. Clarke observes that where the Hebrew has Hebrews the Septuagint read slaves, so that its text must have had a word differing by one letter, a reading no other version or manuscript supports. Keil and Delitzsch explain the two names, those whom the Philistines had absorbed into their army being called Hebrews after the foreign usage and those with the king called Israel after the sacred name, and note that the earlier translators solved the awkward infinitive by interpolating they returned, right in sense though no licence to amend the text. Ellicott takes them for prisoners compelled to fight; John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) allows either constraint or policy, to gain their protection.
24:
The oath is judged four ways, and the judgements run from mild to severe. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) is gentlest: the intention was good and the matter of the obligation not simply unlawful, had it not been so rigorous in excluding all food and in binding the people under pain of an accursed death, a punishment far exceeding the fault. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) treats it as a miscalculation: fearing the enemy would escape, the king made eating before sunset a capital crime and so defeated his own intention, the exhausted people being unable to continue the pursuit. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) allows the royal power and the good motive, then condemns the act on three counts: impolitic, since what it gained in time it lost in strength; imperious, worse than muzzling the ox that treads out the corn, for to forbid feasting would have been commendable but to forbid tasting was barbarous; and impious, for enforcing it with a curse, since superiors may chide and correct but not curse. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) are harshest, calling it no proper attitude towards the Lord but an act of false zeal and a despotic measure, finding the proof in the wording, since till I have avenged myself upon mine enemies shows more regard to his own kingly power than to the kingdom of God. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) has him so bent on vengeance that he grudged his soldiers the necessary rest.

The enlightened eyes are explained from the text and from the body. Keil and Delitzsch set out the two readings: the written text probably gives the eyes became seeing, recovering their power of vision, while the Masoretes substituted a reading from the root meaning to become bright, which is likely correct since the letters are easily transposed. Ellicott agrees it means only the dimness of exhaustion passing, and adds that the Talmud builds a prescription on the verse: whoever suffers from intense hunger should eat honey and other sweet things, as efficacious to restore the light of the eyes.

The evening’s transgression is laid partly at the king’s door. Wesley puts it as an epigram: they who made conscience of the king’s commandment for fear of the curse made no scruple of transgressing God’s; and of the rebuke he adds that the king sees their fault but not his own in giving the occasion of it, which is Henry’s charge too, that he was accessory and had made the Lord’s people transgress. Ellicott quotes Dean Stanley, that the moment the enforced fast was over they flew on the captured cattle like Mussulmans at sunset in Ramazan. Keil and Delitzsch read the rebuke as a charge of faithlessness towards Jehovah, and the stone as the means of letting the blood run off.

The altar closes the section on a crux. Ellicott prefers the margin, that this was what he began to build as an altar, and reports the great Jewish commentators divided: Abarbanel has the king begin but not finish, the Midrash has him begin among the kings of Israel the building of altars, while the received rendering makes it his first public acknowledgment to God. Henry knows the same alternative and draws the sting of it: Saul was turning aside from God and yet began now to build altars, most zealous, as many are, for the form of godliness while denying its power. Keil and Delitzsch doubt it was meant for sacrifice at all, taking it for a memorial of the revelation of God in so marvellous a victory. Clarke notes that Samuel as prophet had hitherto erected the altars, and that the king thought he might erect one without him. John Gill (reformed) takes it for peace offerings in thankfulness, or sin offerings to atone for the people, perhaps both and chiefly the former.
36:
The priest’s intervention is read as courage. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) makes Ahiah the only man in that victorious army who dared, with the bravery which alone proceeds from righteousness, to withstand an imperious sovereign: he doubted whether the wholesale bloodshed of a night pursuit accorded with God’s will, no command to exterminate these Philistines having been given. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) agrees he doubted the propriety of it. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the lesson that princes need such men about them as will be their remembrancers, and notes the king could not for shame refuse the proposal once made.

Why the oracle stayed silent divides them four ways. Henry takes the plain inference: when God denies our prayers it concerns us to ask what sin has provoked him, for his ear is not heavy but sin separates. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say the king was to perceive that guilt rested on the people, a curse to be brought to light as a warning. Ellicott has the questioner conclude, when the gems refused to shine, that a public transgression needed atonement before any answer could be looked for, and observes that the king came at last to see the fault was his own. Clarke denies the premise: Jonathan’s eating the honey was no sin and could not have excited God’s displeasure, since no propitiation was offered for it. He assigns two other causes: that God would not send the people out by night, the king’s motive being perfectly vindictive and the pursuit certain to destroy innocent country people and Israelites living among the Philistines; and that multitudes were at that hour unclean from the blood, and must remain so till evening.

The people’s silence is read two ways, and the readings are opposed. Henry and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) make it loyalty: none who had seen Jonathan eat would inform against him, being satisfied his ignorance excused him and unwilling to expose him for so small an offence. Keil and Delitzsch make it fear, no one answering from terror at the king’s word; and Ellicott, quoting Ewald, speaks of the ominous silence of a horror-stricken people.

The prayer before the lot turns on a word. Ellicott holds the margin’s show the innocent the better and more accurate rendering and gives give a perfect lot as Kimchi’s; Henry knows both and takes either as an air of impartial justice, adding that lots are a solemn appeal to Providence and should be cast with prayer. On the long Greek addition here the witnesses part company: Keil and Delitzsch print it in full and Clarke reproduces its substance as worth having, while Ellicott dismisses it as containing no fact of additional interest.

Sentence and rescue close the section. Henry faults the sentence on three counts: it was passed hastily without consulting the oracle, though Jonathan had a good plea in arrest of judgment, the act not being wrong in itself and the prohibition unknown to him; it was passed in fury, and justice is debased when administered with wrath; and it was backed with a curse on himself which returned on his own head. Keil and Delitzsch put it drily: the thing was not wrong in itself but became so only by the oath, which Jonathan had not heard. Clarke frames the whole as a trial: the king was judge, but the people were the jury, and a righteous and impartial jury brought in a verdict according to the evidence, that no man should die but for a breach of God’s law. Henry has them oppose their oath to the king’s, not by violence but by reason, and reports from Josephus that they prayed Jonathan might be loosed from the curse; John Gill (reformed) adds Abarbanel’s view that the king’s words were not an oath at all but the asseveration of a curse.
47:
What it means that Saul took the kingdom is disputed four ways. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) hold that it was by this victory, which drove Israel’s most obstinate foes home, that he first really secured the regal authority, at variance neither with the choice by lot nor with the confirmation at Gilgal. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) names that reading and prefers another: the verse is a general view of a reign of perpetual wars, introductory to the list that follows — his argument being the Ammonite war, which happened considerably earlier and would be out of place unless the verse is read as a heading. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) takes it of resumption, the administration having been in a manner lost to the Philistines; Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) follows the Targum, that he prospered in his government. John Gill (reformed) gives the Targum too and Kimchi’s sense of being strengthened in it, then adds Abarbanel’s quite different reading: that having followed the herd after his anointing, he now took on the state and majesty of a king and concerned himself no more with his cattle.

One phrase in the summary is unsettled. Of the word rendered he vexed them Ellicott says the exact sense has puzzled all commentators: the Septuagint evidently read a different word, giving he was preserved; the majority of versions and Gesenius yield whithersoever he turned he was victorious; and he calls Luther’s whithersoever he turned he inflicted punishment scholarly, noting that Keil adopts it.

The list of sons raises a gap that each handles differently. Clarke reports Calmet’s solution, that Ishbosheth is absent because he was too young to go to the war and only those who went are named, and then demolishes it in a line: why then mention the daughters and the wife — did they go to the war? Wesley offers the same explanation without misgiving, that only the sons who went into these battles and were slain with their father are given. Keil and Delitzsch judge the reason impossible to determine and suggest the name may simply have dropped out in copying, noting that the Chronicles supply a fourth son under another form of the name. Gill reports Abarbanel’s conjecture that Ishbosheth was borne not by Ahinoam but by another wife, and objects to it himself, that though Saul had a concubine we nowhere read of a second wife. Ellicott passes the gap over and finds the real difficulty in the middle name, which occurs nowhere else but in two genealogies as a son of Asher, and is supposed to be the Abinadab who fell on Gilboa.

The household is sketched briefly and the reign closed. Ellicott notes that nothing is known of the queen beyond her name, reports the surmise that she was of the high priest’s family, the prefix in her name and her father’s being the favourite one in that house, and cites Ewald’s inference from the plainness of the household that there was this one wife and one concubine only; of the general he says the reign’s brilliant campaigns owed much to his skill, and that after Gilboa he was the mainstay of the dead king’s house. Keil and Delitzsch correct the genealogy to read the sons of Abiel rather than the son. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the two threads together: the standing army was filled by taking any strong or valiant man the king saw, exactly as Samuel had said the manner of the king would be; and since the wars never ceased he had little reason to be proud of his dignity, nor his neighbours cause to envy him, for he could not vex his enemies without some vexation to himself — such thorns, he says, are crowns quilted with.
